title: I Hid a Baby Monitor in My Daughter’s Kitchen. Then I Heard a Woman Laugh Who Had Been Dead for Nearly 70 Years.
excerpt: I Hid a Baby Monitor in My Daughter’s Kitchen. Then I Heard a Woman Laugh Who Had Been Dead for Nearly 70 Years.My name is Martha. I'm 76 years old,...
author: admin

blocks.text: My name is Martha. I’m 76 years old, and until three weeks ago, I believed the biggest mistake of my life was trusting my son-in-law.
The biggest mistake was believing that the people who loved me had nothing to hide.

For the past four years, I had lived in a converted den in my daughter Elise’s house. My son-in-law, Gavin, loved telling visitors that he had renovated the room because family should always take care of family.
He never mentioned the $240,000 I had contributed toward purchasing their home.
He never mentioned that I had sold the house where my late husband and I had lived for 27 years to help them afford it.
And he certainly never mentioned that my name was on the deed as a 30% owner.
A separate written agreement guaranteed my right to remain in the converted den for the rest of my life unless I voluntarily chose to leave.
Still, Gavin treated me like an unwanted guest.
He complained when I watched television too loudly. He sighed whenever I cooked something that smelled too strongly. Sometimes, when he thought Elise couldn’t hear him, he called me “the old anchor.”
She was 43, worked long hours at a medical office, and had enough worries of her own.
One evening, I heard Gavin speaking on the phone in the kitchen.
“She’s getting older,” he said. “We can’t keep doing this forever.”
I couldn’t hear the other person’s response.
The following morning, I purchased a small audio baby monitor. I placed the transmitter discreetly near the kitchen and kept the receiver in my room.
Every night, I slipped it beneath my pillow.
And sometimes, when people are frightened, they do things they never imagined themselves capable of doing.
Gavin complained about bills, football, and the price of groceries.
It was shortly after 11:30 when I heard the back door open.
I had known it since I was seven years old.
I remember that morning as clearly as if it happened yesterday.
Evelyn had been playing beside the old pond behind our childhood home. I had been the one who dared her to climb onto the wooden platform.
By the time our father pulled her out, she was gone.
I had spent nearly seven decades believing that my carelessness had killed my sister.
Now I was hearing her laugh in my daughter’s kitchen.
“Traffic. Besides, you should be grateful I came at all.”
“Have you spoken to her?” the woman asked.
“Martha still believes everything you tell her?”
“She’s suspicious, but she’s old. She won’t remember half of what happened.”
Then she said something that made my hands tremble.
“Of course. That’s what she’s believed her entire life.”
“Then we need to make sure she never finds out the truth.”
Because Gavin said something I will never forget.
“Once we get her to sign the paperwork, the house is ours. We can finally sell it without her interfering.”
“After everything we’ve done, she still thinks this is her home.”
The next morning, I waited until Gavin left for work.
“Sweetheart, do you know someone named Evelyn?”
Or she was a better actress than I had ever imagined.
That afternoon, I called an old family friend, Margaret, who had lived two houses away from us when we were children.
I asked her a question I hadn’t asked in almost 70 years.
“Margaret, did they ever find Evelyn’s body?”
“Your parents never identified the little girl they buried.”
“Your sister wasn’t the child who drowned that afternoon.”
“I don’t know. But your parents brought Evelyn away that same night. They told everyone she had died because they were afraid of what would happen if people discovered the truth.”
Before I could ask another question, Margaret added:
At 10:45 p.m., I turned on the receiver.
I heard papers being placed on the kitchen counter.
“Everything is ready. The deed transfer, the medical authorization, and the statement that Martha is voluntarily surrendering her ownership.”
They weren’t simply trying to get rid of me.
They were trying to take my share of the house.
“Then we make her understand that Elise will lose everything if she doesn’t cooperate.”
“Your little investment is safe. Once the house sells, we’ll divide the proceeds.”
Then Gavin asked the question I had been dreading.
“Are you absolutely sure you’re her sister?”
“Look at me, Gavin. I have the same birthmark behind my left ear. I remember our childhood home. I remember the pond. And I remember the day our parents told everyone I was dead.”
“My name is Evelyn. I am Martha’s older sister. And I have spent almost 70 years waiting to come home.”
I didn’t know whether to cry, scream, or laugh.
The little girl I had mourned for nearly seven decades had been living somewhere in the world.
The following morning, I called a lawyer.
